extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and counsel handling claim construction / §112 disputes (especially involving software/means-plus-function claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting disputed patent claim terms and assessing indefiniteness and means-plus-function (§112(f)) issues, with focus on whether claim language, the specification, and disclosed algorithms supply adequate antecedent basis and structure. Applies particularly to software-implemented claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness — Nautilus standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Definiteness requires a claim to “inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.” Nautilus, 572 U.S. at 910.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broader scope alone does not render a claim indefinite. Ambiguities that a PHOSITA might see in the claim language can be resolved by the clarity of the specification. The court should assess whether, reading the claims in light of the specification, a PHOSITA would be reasonably certain of the term’s scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specification / intrinsic evidence to resolve ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are interpreted in light of the specification; a PHOSITA viewing claims “in light of the specification,” would recognize the specification teaches embodiments that clarify ambiguous claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim could plausibly be read multiple ways, the specification may supply antecedent basis or otherwise resolve ambiguity (Med. Co. v. Mylan, DeMarini Sports). Courts should examine specification disclosures (e.g., repeated recitation of RDML) to determine what a PHOSITA would understand the claim to require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis requirement (including implied antecedent basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term may have antecedent basis implied by earlier claim language (e.g., the use of “markup document” in claim 10 provides antecedent basis for 'the markup language' in claim 12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may find antecedent basis based on claim phraseology combined with specification context; antecedent basis need not be explicit if a PHOSITA reading claims and spec would be reasonably certain of the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary characteristics do not necessarily create new claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with secondary characteristics (e.g., XML 1.0 compliance) does not transform an underlying markup language into a different markup language such that claim scope becomes indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between an underlying language (RDML) and optional compliance or secondary characteristics (XML compliance); differences in secondary traits do not alone create different ‘languages’ for claim-scope purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and infringement are distinct from indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of enablement is distinct from indefiniteness; likewise, infringement questions are separate from claim construction/indefiniteness findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid conflating enablement or infringement issues with the legal analysis of definiteness under §112(b) or (a); findings on indefiniteness at claim construction do not resolve enablement or infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function construction: include claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of a means-plus-function claim must be construed to include the limitations contained in the claim language. Lockheed, 324 F.3d at 1319.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may not improperly broaden a means-plus-function claim by ignoring clear limitations in the claim language; any limitation that materially restricts how the function is performed should be included in the recited function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of 'so that' / 'whereby' clauses in function
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a 'so that' (or 'whereby') clause merely states a result or instead substantively limits the manner of performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the clause restricts how the function operates (i.e., requires transformation into a common format or unit), it is a substantive limitation that must be included in the function. If it only states the result of other limitations, it may be excluded (per Lockheed/Texas Instruments precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software means-plus-function: algorithmic disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented means-plus-function claims, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed function such that a PHOSITA would recognize the structure and associate it with the function. (Noah Sys., Net MoneyIN, Aristocrat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosed algorithm may appear in figures and accompanying text describing stepwise procedures (examples: Figures 10 and 11 and associated col./line citations). The specification must disclose steps (not just high-level goals) that map to the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: If no algorithm is disclosed, claim is indefinite under §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification discloses no algorithm for a computer-implemented means-plus-function claim, the inquiry is complete and the claims are indefinite. (CellCast, EON Corp.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should first ask whether any algorithm is disclosed; absence of any algorithmic disclosure mandates indefiniteness. If some algorithm is disclosed, adequacy may be litigated further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of disclosed algorithm — mapping and substeps
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosed algorithm must meaningfully map to the claim's recited function and include necessary substeps; an ad hoc list of special cases or a black-box 'determine desired transformation' is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the specification's algorithm describes how to determine what should be transformed, how to select transformation, and the concrete steps (e.g., accessing attributes, determining conversion factors, multiplying conversion factors, displaying transformed data). Missing substeps or opaque 'secret sauce' determinations support a contention of insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm need not be source code
rubrics_metrics.description: The algorithmic structure supporting a software-implemented claim need not be the operative source code itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level stepwise algorithms in the specification (flowcharts, descriptions of operations) can satisfy the requirement if they are sufficiently specific to associate structure with the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disputes over algorithm adequacy often require expert evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When an algorithm is disclosed but its adequacy is disputed, arguments regarding sufficiency must be evaluated according to expert testimony from a skilled artisan's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties have not conducted expert discovery, courts may defer final adequacy determinations to summary judgment; where expert evidence exists, courts weigh competing expert opinions but should be cautious about relying solely on conclusory expert battles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macros or alternate disclosed elements must show algorithmic detail to qualify as structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged alternate structures (e.g., macros) must themselves be disclosed with algorithmic steps corresponding to the claimed function; mere mentions that macros 'evaluate the transformation string' or update titles/legends do not suffice to show transformation of numerical values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should examine the actual specification passages cited for macros or alternative structures to confirm they disclose the algorithmic steps required by the claim function. If not, those elements cannot be included as structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may identify specific structures from the specification as corresponding to function
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification discloses specific structures with algorithmic descriptions (e.g., RDML data viewer; X-value transformer; Figures and column/line citations), the court can adopt those as the structure corresponding to the means-plus-function limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sufficient algorithmic disclosure exists, the court's final construction should list the identified structures and their supporting specification citations as the means-plus-function structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary vs final construction and limits of claim-construction stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may issue a preliminary construction based on briefs, intrinsic evidence, and hearings, and later refine to a final construction; claims about algorithm adequacy (enablement) may be reserved for later proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At claim construction courts decide scope/definiteness based on intrinsic evidence and may rule the disclosed algorithm is sufficient to avoid indefiniteness without resolving whether the algorithm is enabling; adequacy disputes that depend on factual expert resolution may be left to summary judgment.
